source_read: PMC HTML, PMC4295903 (accepted author manuscript): abstract, all body sections, Tables 1a, 1b and 2 (HTML), Figure 1a, 1b and 2 read on the rendered images, funding, disclosures and contributor statements. Supplementary docx and Figures 3a/3b (supplementary .tif) not opened.

claims.note: The source is cited to qualify the claim and does: it reports an association between METH/AMPH diagnosis codes and later PD codes, and its authors read it as human evidence that preclinical Parkinson-like neurotoxicity 'may be mirrored in humans' (Conclusions 4.4). The data themselves (administrative codes, young ages at diagnosis, no adjustment for tobacco or antipsychotics) do not establish dopamine-neuron damage, so the claim's 'not established' framing stands.

anchors.extracted: Authors state imaging and post-mortem studies indicate persistent dopaminergic deficits and conclude their roughly 3-fold PD/PT risk supports preclinical neurotoxicity findings being mirrored in humans; the study itself measures only ICD-9 diagnosis codes, with the limitations listed in 4.2.

claims.overstatement: 'People with cocaine-related diagnoses showed no increase' is better worded 'no detectable increase': PD/PT HR 0.9 (95% CI 0.3 to 2.4) on 4 vs 22 events, and there was only one PD (332.0) case among cocaine users, so the PD-specific comparison was not estimable. The smoking sentence needs care: the main HRs were indeed not tobacco-adjusted, but smoking is inversely associated with PD (the paper says so), so classical confounding by smoking would bias toward the null; the paper's one tobacco-related result (case-only METH/AMPH vs cocaine, HR 3.9, 1.4-10.8) is printed as 'HRtobacco=1.9 (0.9-4.0)', which is either the tobacco-adjusted exposure HR (halved) or the tobacco code's own HR; under either reading tobacco codes are positively, not inversely, associated with the outcome in these data, which points to ascertainment (more medical contact) rather than to smoking causing PD. 'Unadjusted smoking' is accurate for the main HRs, but the editors may want to name ascertainment/healthcare contact as the mechanism.
claims.note: All counts and estimates from this source match: n=4,935; 5:1 matched controls n=24,675; PD events 15 vs 27; HR 2.8 (1.6-4.8); PD/PT 30 vs 49, HR 3.1; mean follow-up 6.8 years; few levodopa orders. Editors' absolute risks recomputed: 15/4,935 = 0.30% vs 27/24,675 = 0.11%, difference 1.9 per 1,000 (crude cumulative proportions; controls' mean follow-up 7.1 years; competing deaths 5.8% vs 0.4% ignored) - same as the claim. Part not supported as worded: the 'median age of 49' and 'about 2 years' are Table 1a values for the broader PD/PT outcome (30 events), not for PD codes (15 events), and the 2.0 years is a mean (SD 1.8) measured from the first METH/AMPH code (the paper's event time; 8 of 30 PD/PT cases were coded on the same date as exposure), not from the study baseline of 1 January 1996. The California HR is described here only as '1.8-fold' vs appendicitis controls (Introduction), consistent with 1.76.

anchors.extracted: METH/AMPH cohort: anyone born 1940 or later, aged 30+ by end-2011, with ICD-9-CM 304.4, 305.7, 969.7 or E854.2, and no HIV, no prior PD/PT, and no other illicit-drug or alcohol codes: 16,931 identified, 11,985 (71%) removed for other drug/alcohol codes, 11 for prior PD/PT, leaving 4,935. 305.7 (amphetamine or related sympathomimetic abuse) present in 72%. Controls: 24,675 drawn from 1.43 million unexposed residents, matched 5:1 on sex and birth year with at least equal follow-up. Mean follow-up 6.8 (SD 4.3) years in users, 7.1 (4.3) in controls; median age at follow-up 40 vs 42.

PD (332.0): 15 events in users vs 27 in controls, HR 2.8 (95% CI 1.6 to 4.8), p<0.001 (competing-risks model with death; individual matching). By sex: women 8 vs 6, HR 6.7 (2.7-16.2); men 7 vs 21, HR 1.7 (0.8-3.5, p=0.18).

PD/PT (332.0, 332.1, 333.0, 333.1): 30 vs 49 events, HR 3.1 (95% CI 2.1 to 4.5) in Results text and Figure 1b; the Abstract prints 1.9 to 4.9 for the same estimate. Women HR 5.0 (2.9-8.6), men 1.9 (1.1-3.5); case-only women vs men 1.7 (0.8-3.6, p=0.15).

Cocaine-only cohort (n=1,867; 9,335 controls): PD/PT 4 vs 22 events, HR 0.9 (0.3 to 2.4, p=0.85); only one cocaine case had a 332.0 code. Case-only METH/AMPH vs cocaine HR 3.9 (1.4 to 10.8); the tobacco result is printed as 'HRtobacco=1.9 (0.9 to 4.0), P=0.01, data not shown' - ambiguous between the adjusted exposure HR and the tobacco covariate's HR, and the p-value is incompatible with the interval.

anchors.locator: Table 1a (Age, index PD/PT diagnosis; Years to index PD/PT diagnosis); Methods 2.3.1; Results 3.2, para 3
anchors.extracted: In users with a PD/PT outcome: median age at index diagnosis 49 (range 25-69) vs 44 (20-68) in controls; mean 2.0 (SD 1.8) years to index PD/PT diagnosis vs 2.9 (3.5). Outcomes coded on the same day as the first exposure code were counted; excluding them left 12 PD and 22 PD/PT cases, HR 2.2 (1.2-4.0) and 2.3 (1.5-3.5).

anchors.locator: Results 3.1, final para; Discussion 4.2, paras 2 and 4; Methods 2.3.3; Table 1a (smoking)
anchors.extracted: Carbidopa-levodopa ordered for 3 users and 5 controls with incident PD/PT (limited medication data). ICD-9 codes for PD are imperfect (single 332.0 code PPV 57%, 332.1 39% in one validation study; broader code sets lower PPV); antipsychotic exposure, which can cause drug-induced parkinsonism, was not controlled; tobacco code in 58.6% of users vs 8.3% of controls, and the main METH/AMPH-vs-control models were not tobacco-adjusted; race/ethnicity not adjusted.

key_findings.correction: The discrepancy can be resolved from the rendered Figure 1b: overall PD/PT HR 3.1, p<0.0001, 95% CI 2.1 to 4.5, matching the Results; the abstract's 1.9-4.9 is the outlier.

Person-year rates recomputed (2.68 vs 2.71 per 10,000). The HR is readable on the rendered Figure 2: cocaine vs controls PD/PT HR 0.9 (95% CI 0.3 to 2.4), p=0.85; case-only cocaine vs METH/AMPH 0.3 (0.1 to 0.7).

'Did not substantively change it' is the authors' statement; as the card's analysis field notes, 'HRtobacco=1.9 (0.9-4.0)' may be the tobacco covariate's own HR, and if it is the adjusted exposure HR it is half the unadjusted 3.9 with an interval including 1, so the authors' statement is not verifiable.
Recomputed: 0.304% vs 0.109% (1.95 per 1,000); 4.47 vs 1.54 per 10,000 person-years; broader outcome 0.608% vs 0.199% (4.1 per 1,000), 8.9 vs 2.8 per 10,000 person-years.

Table 1a does not say what the 'years to index PD/PT diagnosis' are measured from, and both rows refer to the PD/PT outcome (30 exposed events), not PD. The paper's event time for exposed people starts at the first METH/AMPH code (same-date outcomes are 'zero event times', Methods 2.3.1; Results 3.2 para 3), so the 2.0 years (SD 1.8) is most plausibly the interval from the first exposure code to the PD/PT code, not from the study baseline of 1 January 1996. The card's 'from baseline' (and the claim's 'about 2 years after baseline') should be reworded.

reporting_issues.note: Figure 1b (rendered) gives 2.1-4.5, so the Results are right and the abstract is wrong.
173/2,399 = 7.2%; 88.7 + 7.2 + 4.1 = 100. The card's explanatory clause is garbled but the issue is correct.

The estimates are not extractable from the text, but the rendered figures print them legibly: Figure 1a PD women 6.7 (2.7-16.2), men 1.7 (0.8-3.5, p=0.18), case-only women vs men 1.3 (0.5-3.5, p=0.63); Figure 1b PD/PT case-only women vs men 1.7 (0.8-3.6, p=0.15); Figure 2 cocaine vs controls 0.9 (0.3-2.4, p=0.85). The cocaine null does have a printed interval, inside the figure.
Also: the control range for age at follow-up is printed as 29-71 although inclusion required age 30 or older.
The paper itself cites the essential-tremor/PD confusion (Louis et al.); 'tremor is a recognized effect of stimulant use' is the card's addition, not stated in the paper.

risk_of_bias.note: Domain judgments agreed. The overall label is inconsistent with them: ROBINS-E overall risk should be at least as severe as the worst domain, and the card rates Measurement of the outcome 'high', so the overall should be 'high' (ROBINS-E uses low / some concerns / high / very high; 'serious' is ROBINS-I wording). Same reasoning text applies.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' agreed: abstract and Conclusions ('Parkinson-like neurotoxicity may be mirrored in humans') go beyond coded associations at a median age of 49 with few levodopa orders.

missed: Rendered Figures 1a, 1b and 2 give the estimates the card treats as unavailable (listed under reporting issue 4); in particular the narrow PD outcome in men was not significant (HR 1.7, 0.8-3.5) and the female-male case-only comparison for PD was HR 1.3 (0.5-3.5).

For cl_meth_parkinson: the claim's 'median age of 49, about 2 years after baseline' uses Table 1a values that belong to the PD/PT composite (30 events), not to PD (15 events), and the 2.0 years is a mean measured from the first exposure code; the sentence should be reworded accordingly.

Introduction describes Callaghan et al.'s California estimate as '1.8-fold' vs appendicitis controls from statewide inpatient and death records 1990-2005, while Discussion 4.1 calls it 'a northern California population'; minor internal inconsistency, relevant if Curtin is used as the secondary source for the California HR.

Discussion 4.2 answers the antipsychotic concern by citing Bramness et al. (2012) that psychotic complications subside quickly; that addresses psychosis being mistaken for PD, not antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism being coded as PD/PT, which remains unaddressed.
